New Orleans is located along the Mississippi River in the southeastern region of the U.S. state of Louisiana.
New Orleans is the most populous city in Louisiana and the French Louisiana region; third most populous city in the Deep South; and the twelfth-most populous city in the southeastern United States.
New Orleans serves as a major port, considered an economic and commercial hub for the broader Gulf Coast region of the United States.
New Orleans is world-renowned for its distinctive music, Creole cuisine, unique dialects, and annual celebrations and festivals, most notably Mardi Gras.
The historic heart of New Orleans is the French Quarter, known for its French and Spanish Creole architecture and vibrant nightlife along Bourbon Street.
New Orleans has been described as "the most unique" in the United States due to its cross-cultural and multilingual heritage.
New Orleans is increasingly known as "Hollywood South" due to its prominent role in the film industry and pop culture.
New Orleans was founded in 1718 by French colonists.
New Orleans was once the territorial capital of French Louisiana before becoming part of the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.
In 1840, New Orleans was the third most populous city in the United States and the largest city in the American South from the Antebellum era until after World War II.
New Orleans has historically been very vulnerable to flooding due to its high rainfall, low-lying elevation, poor natural drainage, and proximity to multiple bodies of water.
State and federal authorities have installed a complex system of levees and drainage pumps to protect New Orleans from flooding.

Hurricane Katrina severely affected New Orleans in late August 2005, flooding more than 80% of the city, killing over 1,800 people, and displacing thousands of residents, causing a population decline of over 50%.
Since Katrina, major redevelopment efforts have led to a rebound in the city's population.
Concerns have been expressed about gentrification, new residents buying property in formerly close-knit communities, and displacement of longtime residents.
High rates of violent crime continue to plague New Orleans with 280 murders in 2022, resulting in the highest per capita homicide rate in the United States.
The city anchors the larger Greater New Orleans metropolitan area, which had a population of 1,271,845 in 2020.
Greater New Orleans is the most populous metropolitan statistical area (MSA) in Louisiana and, since the 2020 census, has been the 46th most populous MSA in the United States.
The name of New Orleans derives from the original French name (La Nouvelle-Orléans), which was given to the city in honor of Philippe II, Duke of Orléans.
Philippe II, Duke of Orléans served as regent of the Kingdom of France from 1715 to 1723.
The French city of Orléans itself is named after the Roman emperor Aurelian.
New Orleans is also named after Aurelian, so its name in Latin would translate to Nova Aurelia.
La Nouvelle-Orléans (New Orleans) was founded in the spring of 1718 by the French Mississippi Company under the direction of Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville.
The Chitimacha inhabited the land where New Orleans was founded.
The city was named for Philippe II, Duke of Orléans.
Philippe II, Duke of Orléans' title came from the French city of Orléans.

The French colony of Louisiana was ceded to Spain in 1763 following France's defeat by Great Britain in the Seven Years' War.
During the American Revolutionary War, New Orleans served as an important port for smuggling aid to revolutionaries and transporting military equipment up the Mississippi River.
Beginning in the 1760s, Filipinos began to settle in and around New Orleans.
Bernardo de Gálvez y Madrid, Count of Gálvez successfully directed a southern campaign against the British from New Orleans in 1779.
Nueva Orleans (the name of New Orleans in Spanish) remained under Spanish control until 1803 when it reverted briefly to French rule.

Inability to find labor was the most pressing issue in the young colony, leading to the importation of sub-Saharan African slaves to make investments profitable.
The transatlantic slave trade imported enslaved Africans into Louisiana in the late 1710s.
This led to the biggest shipment in 1716 where several trading ships appeared with slaves as cargo over a one-year span.
By 1724, large numbers of blacks in Louisiana prompted the institutionalizing of laws governing slavery within the colony.
These laws required that slaves be baptized in the Roman Catholic faith and married in the church.
The slave law formed in the 1720s is known as the Code Noir.
Louisiana slave culture had its own distinct Afro-Creole society that called on past cultures and the situation for slaves in the New World.
Afro-Creole was present in religious beliefs and the Louisiana Creole language.
The religion most associated with this period was called Voodoo.
French policy-makers in Paris attempted to set political and economic norms for New Orleans, but it stayed in communication with foreign trends as well.
After the French relinquished West Louisiana to Spain, New Orleans merchants attempted to ignore Spanish rule and even re-institute French control on the colony.
The citizens of New Orleans held a series of public meetings during 1765 to keep the populace opposed to the establishment of Spanish rule.
The Third Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1800 restored French control of New Orleans and Louisiana, but Napoleon sold both to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.
Thereafter, the city grew rapidly with influxes of Americans, French, Creoles, and Africans.
Later immigrants were Irish, Germans, Poles, and Italians.
Major commodity crops of sugar and cotton were cultivated on nearby large plantations using slave labor.
Between 1791 and 1810, thousands of St. Domingue refugees arrived in New Orleans; a number brought their slaves with them.
The port handled commodities for export from the interior and imported goods from other countries, which were warehoused and transferred to smaller vessels along the Mississippi River watershed.
Despite its role in the slave trade, New Orleans at the time also had the largest and most prosperous community of free persons of color in the nation.
Dwarfing the other cities in the Antebellum South, New Orleans had the U.S.'s largest slave market.
The market expanded after the United States ended the international trade in 1808.
Two-thirds of the more than one million slaves brought to the Deep South arrived via forced migration in the domestic slave trade.
The money generated by the sale of slaves in the Upper South has been estimated at 15 percent of the value of the staple crop economy, with slaves collectively valued at half a billion dollars.

The trade spawned an ancillary economy—transportation, housing and clothing, fees, etc., estimated at 13.5 percent of the price per person, amounting to tens of billions of dollars (2005 dollars, adjusted for inflation) during the antebellum period.
The addition of white immigrants from Saint-Domingue to the white creole population enabled French-speakers to remain a majority of the white population until almost 1830.
If a substantial proportion of free persons of color and slaves had not also spoken French, the Gallic community would have become a minority of the total population as early as 1820.
After the Louisiana Purchase, numerous Anglo-Americans migrated to New Orleans.
The population doubled in the 1830s and by 1840, New Orleans had become the nation's wealthiest city after New York and Baltimore.
German and Irish immigrants began arriving in the 1840s, working as port laborers.
In the 1850s, white Francophones remained an intact and vibrant community in New Orleans.
They maintained instruction in French in two of the city's four school districts (all served white students).
In 1860, the city had 13,000 free people of color, constituting the artisan, educated, and professional class of African Americans.
Throughout New Orleans' history until the early 20th century, the city suffered repeated epidemics of yellow fever and other tropical and infectious diseases.
In the first half of the 19th century, yellow fever epidemics killed over 150,000 people in New Orleans.
After growing by 45 percent in the 1850s, by 1860, the city had nearly 170,000 people.
It had grown in wealth with a "per capita income" that was second in the nation and the highest in the South.
The port was the nation's third largest in terms of tonnage of imported goods after Boston and New York.

New Orleans residents supportive of the Confederacy nicknamed him "Beast" Butler because of an order he issued.
Butler abolished French-language instruction in city schools.
Significantly, Butler also came to be called "Spoons" Butler due to alleged looting by his troops during their occupation of the city.
By the end of the 19th century, French usage had faded and was under pressure from Irish, Italian, and German immigrants.

Most of the southern portion of Louisiana was originally exempted from the liberating provisions of the 1863 Emancipation Proclamation issued by President Abraham Lincoln.
Large numbers of rural ex-slaves and some free people of color from the city volunteered for the first regiments of Black troops in the War.

While that name had been used before the war, this group was made up mostly of former slaves.
Violence throughout the South, especially the Memphis Riots of 1866 and the New Orleans Riot in the same year, led Congress to pass the Reconstruction Act and the Fourteenth Amendment.
Louisiana and Texas were put under the authority of the "Fifth Military District" of the United States during Reconstruction.
In 1872, lieutenant governor P.B.S. Pinchback succeeded Henry Clay Warmouth for a brief period as Republican governor of Louisiana, becoming the first governor of African descent of a U.S. state.

In 1892, one of New Orleans' large community of well-educated free persons of color (gens de couleur libres) organized the Comité des Citoyens to work for civil rights.
As part of their legal campaign, they recruited Homer Plessy to test Louisiana's newly enacted Separate Car Act.
Plessy boarded a commuter train departing New Orleans for Covington and was arrested.
The case resulting from this incident, Plessy v. Ferguson, was heard by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1896.
The court ruled that "separate but equal" accommodations were constitutional.
In practice, African American public schools and facilities were underfunded across the South.
The Supreme Court ruling contributed to this period as the nadir of race relations in the United States.
The rate of lynchings of black men was high across the South.
Anti-Italian sentiment in 1891 contributed to the lynching of 11 Italians, some of whom had been acquitted of the murder of the police chief.
Some were shot and killed in the jail where they were detained. It was the largest mass lynching in U.S. history.

New Orleanians recognized that their city was no longer the leading urban area in the South by the mid-20th century.
By 1950, Houston, Dallas, and Atlanta exceeded New Orleans in size.
In 1960, Miami eclipsed New Orleans, even as its population reached its historic peak.
Suburban development drew residents from the center city to newer housing outside.
The 1970 census recorded the first absolute decline in population since the city became part of the United States in 1803.

Hurricanes pose a severe threat to the area due to its low elevation and surrounding water from the north, east, and south.
According to the Federal Emergency Management Agency, New Orleans is the nation's most vulnerable city to hurricanes.
New Orleans was catastrophically affected by Hurricane Katrina on August 29, 2005, when the federal levee system failed during the hurricane.
By the time the hurricane approached the city that day, most residents had evacuated.
The majority of the city remained dry as floodwalls and levees constructed by the United States Army Corps of Engineers failed below design specifications.
More than 1,500 people were recorded as having died in Louisiana, most in New Orleans, while others remain unaccounted for.
Before Hurricane Katrina, the city called for the first mandatory evacuation in its history to be followed by another mandatory evacuation three years later with Hurricane Gustav.
The city was declared off-limits to residents while efforts to clean up after Hurricane Katrina began.
The approach of Hurricane Rita in September 2005 caused repopulation efforts to be postponed, and the Lower Ninth Ward was reflooded by Rita's storm surge.
Because of the scale of damage, many people resettled permanently outside the area.
Federal, state, and local efforts supported recovery and rebuilding in severely damaged neighborhoods.

The U.S. Census Bureau estimated the population to be 223,000 in July 2006; a subsequent study estimated that 32,000 additional residents had moved to the city as of March 2007, bringing the estimated population to 255,000.
Another estimate based on utility usage from July 2007 estimated the population to be approximately 274,000 or 60% of the pre-Katrina population.
A third estimate based on mail delivery records in June 2007 indicated that the city had regained approximately two-thirds of its pre-Katrina population.
In 2008, the U.S. Census Bureau revised its population estimate for the city upward to 336,644.
